{{Short description|Mathematical Banach space}}
{{more footnotes|date=September 2025}}
In [[mathematics]] &mdash; specifically, in [[functional analysis]] &mdash; an '''Asplund space''' or '''strong differentiability space''' is a type of [[well-behaved]] [[Banach space]].  Asplund spaces were introduced in 1968 by the [[mathematician]] [[Edgar Asplund]], who was interested in the [[Fréchet derivative|Fréchet differentiability]] properties of [[Lipschitz function]]s on Banach spaces.

==Equivalent definitions==

There are many equivalent definitions of what it means for a Banach space ''X'' to be an '''Asplund space''':
* ''X'' is Asplund if and only if every [[separable space|separable subspace]] ''Y'' of ''X'' has separable [[continuous dual space]] ''Y''<sup>∗</sup>.
* ''X'' is Asplund if and only if every [[continuous function|continuous]] [[convex function]] on any [[open set|open]] [[convex set|convex subset]] ''U'' of ''X'' is Fréchet differentiable at the points of a [[dense set|dense]] [[Gδ set|''G''<sub>''δ''</sub>-subset]] of ''U''.
* ''X'' is Asplund if and only if its dual space ''X''<sup>∗</sup> has the [[Radon–Nikodym property|Radon–Nikodým property]].  This property was established by Namioka & Phelps in 1975 and Stegall in 1978.
* ''X'' is Asplund if and only if every non-empty [[bounded set|bounded subset]] of its dual space ''X''<sup>∗</sup> has [[weak topology|weak-∗-slices]] of arbitrarily small diameter.
* ''X'' is Asplund if and only if every non-empty weakly-∗ [[compact set|compact]] [[convex set|convex]] subset of the dual space ''X''<sup>∗</sup> is the weakly-∗ closed [[convex hull]] of its weakly-∗ strongly [[exposed point]]s.  In 1975, Huff & Morris showed that this property is equivalent to the statement that every bounded, closed and convex subset of the dual space ''X''<sup>∗</sup> is closed convex hull of its extreme points.

==Properties of Asplund spaces==

* The class of Asplund spaces is closed under topological isomorphisms:  that is, if ''X'' and ''Y'' are Banach spaces, ''X'' is Asplund, and ''X'' is [[homeomorphic]] to ''Y'', then ''Y'' is also an Asplund space.
* Every [[closed set|closed]] [[linear subspace]] of an Asplund space is an Asplund space.
* Every [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient space]] of an Asplund space is an Asplund space.
* The class of Asplund spaces is closed under extensions:  if ''X'' is a Banach space and ''Y'' is an Asplund subspace of ''X'' for which the quotient space ''X''&nbsp;⁄&nbsp;''Y'' is Asplund, then ''X'' is Asplund.
* Every locally Lipschitz function on an open subset of an Asplund space is Fréchet differentiable at the points of some dense subset of its domain.  This result was established by [[David Preiss|Preiss]] in 1990 and has applications in optimization theory.
* The following theorem from Asplund's original 1968 paper is a good example of why non-Asplund spaces are badly behaved:  if ''X'' is not an Asplund space, then there exists an equivalent norm on ''X'' that fails to be Fréchet differentiable at every point of ''X''.
* In 1976, Ekeland & Lebourg showed that if ''X'' is a Banach space that has an equivalent norm that is Fréchet differentiable away from the origin, then ''X'' is an Asplund space.  However, in 1990, Haydon gave an example of an Asplund space that does not have an equivalent norm that is [[Gateaux derivative|Gateaux differentiable]] away from the origin.
